hints: Start with the tiniest one, the polio virus at about 30 nm. Which structure in the table is famously the smallest of all, so small you need an electron microscope to see it clearly?
Remember the size ladder in micrometres: ribosome is about 0.02 um, lysosome is about 0.5 um, mitochondrion is about 1 um, nucleus is about 10 um. Convert the three viruses to um to match them up.
walkthrough:
**Put the viruses in size order**

Great start, let's just look at the numbers first. Polio is tiny at about $30\text{ nm}$, Mimivirus is medium at about $680\text{ nm}$, and Pandoravirus is large at about $1000\text{ nm}$.

Remember the handy conversion:
$$1000\text{ nm} = 1\text{ }\mu\text{m}$$

**Recall your cell structure sizes**

Now think like a biologist. Ribosomes are the smallest, about $20\text{ to }30\text{ nm}$ in diameter. Lysosomes are small vesicles, about $100\text{ to }500\text{ nm}$. Mitochondria are much bigger, about $1000\text{ nm}$ ($1\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) wide. The nucleus is huge, about $10\text{ }\mu\text{m}$.

**Match smallest to smallest**

Polio ($30\text{ nm}$) matches the ribosome ($20\text{ to }30\text{ nm}$) perfectly. Mimivirus ($680\text{ nm}$) is closest to a lysosome. Pandoravirus ($1000\text{ nm} = 1\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) is closest to a mitochondrion in width. That gives ribosome, lysosome, mitochondrion.

options.A: Incorrect, as a lysosome (hundreds of nm) is far too big to match polio virus (30 nm), and a nucleus (about 10 um) is far too big to match Pandoravirus (1 um).
options.B: Incorrect, as a nucleolus is part of the nucleus and is micrometres in size, so it cannot match the tiny 30 nm polio virus.
options.C: Incorrect, as it swaps the last two. Mimivirus (680 nm) is smaller than a mitochondrion (about 1000 nm) and Pandoravirus (1000 nm) is larger than a typical lysosome.
options.D: Correct and well done. Ribosome matches polio (both about 20 to 30 nm), lysosome matches Mimivirus (both hundreds of nm), and mitochondrion matches Pandoravirus (both about 1000 nm or 1 um).
